lessonTitle: Writing a Prescription: Essential Elements, Generic Names and Dose Units

blocks.text: A junior doctor handwrites a dose as .5 mg. The decimal point is faint, the nurse reads 5 mg, and the patient receives ten times the intended amount. Nothing about the drug or the patient was wrong; the harm came from how three characters were written. A prescription is a legal, clinical instruction that must be impossible to misread.

blocks.markdown: A **prescription** is a written instruction from an authorised prescriber to supply and administer a medicine. In hospital it appears on a drug chart (inpatient medication chart) or an electronic prescribing system. Errors at the prescribing stage are among the most common causes of avoidable medication harm, so every element must be complete, legible and unambiguous.

blocks.title: Essential elements of an inpatient prescription
blocks.text: A complete inpatient prescription includes: patient identifiers (full name, date of birth and hospital number); allergy and adverse reaction status; weight where relevant; the drug (approved generic name); dose with unit; route; frequency (and timing where relevant); start date, and stop date or review date (essential for antibiotics); indication where appropriate; and the prescriber's legible signature, printed name and contact details.

blocks.caption: Safe prescribing conventions (following UK practice such as the BNF and national guidance).
rows: Approved generic (non-proprietary) name, for example paracetamol
Avoids duplication and confusion; allows substitution
mcg, ug or the Greek letter mu
Misread as mg, with a 1000-fold error
U can be misread as a zero
Missed decimal point gives a 10-fold overdose
Use mg where possible: 400 mg or 0.5 mg
Mixed units on one chart, such as 0.5 g and 500 mg
Misreading of drug names and doses

blocks.title: Correcting a flawed prescription
blocks.prompt: An order reads: 'digoxin .25mg od oral (ward 4)'. List the problems and rewrite it correctly. (Teaching example only; the dose is for illustration.)

steps.text: Dose format: '.25 mg' lacks a leading zero, so it could be read as 25 mg. Also, 0.25 mg is better written as 250 micrograms in full to avoid decimals.
Frequency: 'od' is an ambiguous abbreviation (it can be misread as 'right eye'); write 'once daily'.
Missing elements: no patient identifiers, allergy status, start date, signature or indication on the order.
Rewrite: Digoxin 250 micrograms, oral, once daily; start date; with patient identifiers, allergy status, signature and printed name.

blocks.answer: Digoxin 250 micrograms oral once daily, with full patient details, allergy status, start date and signature

blocks.markdown: **Generic names.** Drugs have an approved (generic) name, such as the International Nonproprietary Name, and one or more brand names. Prescribing by generic name avoids a patient receiving two brands of the same drug, allows any equivalent product to be supplied and reduces confusion between similar-sounding brands. Exceptions include drugs where the brand matters clinically, such as some modified-release products or biological medicines, where brand prescribing is appropriate.

**Unit conversion.** The metric system is based on powers of 1000. **1 g = 1000 mg; 1 mg = 1000 micrograms; 1 microgram = 1000 nanograms.** Moving from a larger unit to a smaller one multiplies by 1000; going the other way divides by 1000. Concentrations such as '250 micrograms per mL' must be converted to a common unit before calculating a volume to administer.

blocks.caption: Dose required and concentration must be in the same units; the volume is then in the volume unit of the concentration (for example mL).

blocks.title: Unit conversion and volume to draw up
blocks.prompt: A drug is supplied as 400 micrograms in 2 mL. A prescription is for 0.3 mg. Calculate the dose in micrograms and the volume to give. (Teaching example.)

steps.text: Convert the prescribed dose to micrograms: 0.3 mg x 1000 = 300 micrograms.
Find the concentration: 400 micrograms in 2 mL = 200 micrograms per mL.
Check for plausibility: 1.5 mL is less than the 2 mL ampoule, and 300 is three-quarters of 400, so the answer is sensible.

items: Always check allergy status before prescribing, and record the reaction type.
Write the route clearly (oral, intravenous, subcutaneous) because the same drug may be dangerous by the wrong route.
Avoid abbreviations of drug names and frequencies; write 'once daily' rather than 'od'.
Specify stop or review dates, particularly for antibiotics and short courses.
Re-read the order and check the arithmetic, especially for children and for weight-based doses.

blocks.title: Thousand-fold errors
blocks.text: Confusion between micrograms, milligrams and grams produces errors of 1000-fold. Always write 'micrograms' and 'nanograms' in full, and check any dose that is surprisingly large or small.

blocks.title: Quick check
blocks.text: To convert mg to micrograms, move the decimal point three places to the right; to convert micrograms to mg, move it three places to the left.

points: A complete inpatient prescription includes patient identifiers, allergies, drug (generic name), dose with units, route, frequency, start and stop dates and a clear signature.
Use approved generic names, write micrograms and units in full, use a leading zero (0.5 mg) and avoid trailing zeros (5 mg).
1 g = 1000 mg = 1,000,000 micrograms; convert to a common unit before calculating volumes or doses.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an essential element of a complete inpatient prescription?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: allergy status must be recorded to avoid harm from a known allergen.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: the generic name should be used.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: not a required prescription element.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: cost is not part of a prescription.

questions.explanation: A prescription must record the patient's identifiers and allergy status so that the drug, dose, route and frequency are safe for that individual. Brand names, next of kin and cost are not required.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the safest way to prescribe a dose of 62.5 micrograms of digoxin?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: micrograms is written in full.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: mcg is a recognised hazard abbreviation and can be misread as mg.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: ug can be misread as mg.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: lacks a leading zero and uses an awkward decimal.

questions.explanation: Writing micrograms in full removes the risk of misreading abbreviations as mg, which would lead to a 1000-fold error. Using a smaller unit rather than a long decimal also avoids confusion.

questions.stem: A doctor writes the order 'Panadol 1 g four times daily'. What is the main concern about the drug name?

options.text: A generic name (paracetamol) should be used, which avoids duplication with other paracetamol-containing products
Brand names are legally forbidden on all charts
The drug has no generic name
The dose should be given in micrograms

questions.correctOptionText: A generic name (paracetamol) should be used, which avoids duplication with other paracetamol-containing products

distractorRationale.a: Correct: approved generic names reduce duplication and confusion.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: brands are not always forbidden, but generic names are standard practice.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: paracetamol is the generic name.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: 1 g is an appropriate unit for this dose.

questions.explanation: Prescribing by approved generic name helps staff recognise the active ingredient and avoid giving two products containing the same drug. It also allows any suitable equivalent product to be supplied.

questions.stem: A prescription is written for digoxin 0.125 mg. Convert this dose to micrograms.
questions.explanation: 1 mg = 1000 micrograms, so 0.125 mg x 1000 = 125 micrograms. Converting to micrograms removes the leading-zero decimal and reduces the risk of misreading.

questions.stem: A drug is supplied as a solution containing 250 micrograms per mL. A prescriber orders a dose of 0.5 mg. Calculate the volume to give in mL. (Teaching example.)
questions.explanation: Convert the dose to micrograms: 0.5 mg x 1000 = 500 micrograms. Volume = 500 / 250 = 2 mL. Using a common unit for dose and concentration is essential.

questions.stem: A medication is supplied in 500 microgram tablets. A prescriber wants to give 1.5 mg once daily. How many tablets are needed per dose? (Teaching example.)
questions.explanation: 1.5 mg = 1500 micrograms. Dividing by the tablet strength of 500 micrograms gives 3 tablets per dose. A check of plausibility confirms 3 x 500 = 1500 micrograms.

questions.stem: Why is the dose '5.0 mg' considered unsafe on a prescription?

options.text: The decimal point can be missed, leading to the dose being read as 50 mg
It is not a metric dose

questions.correctOptionText: The decimal point can be missed, leading to the dose being read as 50 mg

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a missed decimal turns 5.0 into 50, a tenfold overdose.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: mg is a metric unit.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: trailing zeros should be avoided.

questions.explanation: A trailing zero invites misreading if the decimal point is faint or lost on copying. Writing 5 mg avoids the risk of a tenfold overdose.

questions.stem: List the essential elements of a complete inpatient prescription and explain why each matters for safety.
markingGuide: Patient identifiers (name, date of birth, hospital number) to ensure the right patient
Allergy and adverse reaction status to avoid known allergens
Approved generic drug name to avoid duplication and confusion
Dose with unit, route and frequency to specify exactly what is to be given
Start date and stop or review date (especially antibiotics) to limit unnecessary treatment
Prescriber's legible signature, printed name and contact details for accountability and queries
questions.explanation: Each element closes a specific route to error, from wrong patient to wrong dose or duration. A prescription is also a legal record of the prescriber's decision.

questions.stem: Explain why approved generic names and unambiguous dose units are used in prescriptions, giving three examples of unsafe writing and their safe alternatives.
markingGuide: Generic names identify the active ingredient, avoid duplication of brands, and allow equivalent supply
Micrograms and nanograms should be written in full because mcg or ug can be misread as mg
Missing leading zero (.5 mg) can be read as 5 mg; write 0.5 mg
Trailing zero (5.0 mg) can be read as 50 mg; write 5 mg
'U' for units can be misread as 0; write 'units' in full
Ambiguous frequency abbreviations should be written in full (once daily)
questions.explanation: The goal is that no plausible misreading changes the dose, drug or timing. Misreadings of units and decimals can lead to errors of 10-fold or 1000-fold.

questions.stem: True or false: it is acceptable on a prescription to abbreviate micrograms as 'mcg'.
questions.explanation: Micrograms should be written in full because abbreviations such as mcg can be mistaken for mg, causing a 1000-fold overdose. This is a standard safe-prescribing convention.
